\chapter{Family and Friend}
\label{ch:ml-family-and-friend}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my family as a group and name a friend in Malayalam, and say which of the two words is a Sanskrit loan and which of Malayalam's two friend-words leans on a borrowed ending even though its root is native.}

Say ithu ente kudumbamaanu and ithu ente suhruthaanu, take suhruthu apart into su plus hrid, and name the six Chapter 12 people-words next to the one group-word none of them supplied.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuṭumbaṁ]{\ml{കുടുംബം} (kuṭumbaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} the word the six people-words never needed}

\label{lesson:ML-C35-kudumbam}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Enikku malayāḷaṁ iṣṭamāṇŭ} closed the last chapter on a sentence built from nothing but nouns and a dative. This chapter opens on the plainest nouns of all: the people you would actually say it to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കുടുംബം}} — \emph{kuṭumbaṁ} — \textbf{family}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{കുടുംബമാണ്}.} — \emph{ithu ente kuṭumbamāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my family.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ente}, \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} has been yours since your very first sentences; \textbf{‑\ml{ആണ്}} is the same copula that closed \emph{enikku malayāḷaṁ iṣṭamāṇŭ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{കുടുംബം}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{तत्सम} \dv{कुटुम्ब}} (\emph{kuṭumba}), \textquotedblleft{}family, household,\textquotedblright{} absorbed with the same nativizing \textbf{‑\ml{അം}} ending you already met on \textbf{\ml{ഇഷ്ടം}} and \textbf{\ml{സുഖം}} — a genuine Malayalam habit: dress a bare Sanskrit neuter stem in Malayalam's own \textbf{‑aṁ}. Kannada borrows the identical word \textbf{bare}, \textbf{\ka{ಕುಟುಂಬ}} (\emph{kuṭumba}), no ending added — one more place Malayalam leans harder into Sanskrit than its sisters do, this time in the shape of the loan rather than the fact of it.

You already have six words for six specific people: \textbf{\ml{അച്ഛൻ}}, \textbf{\ml{അമ്മ}}, and the four age-graded siblings \textbf{\ml{ചേട്ടൻ}/\ml{അനിയൻ}}, \textbf{\ml{ചേച്ചി}/\ml{അനിയത്തി}}. Every one is native Dravidian, and not one of them means \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{} — each names a single, specific person. Malayalam never inherited a word for the group itself, so when it needed one, it reached for Sanskrit. The people came first, and stayed native; the collective came later, and came borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ithu ente kuṭumbamāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — this is my family
  \item the six named people, then the borrowed group word — \textquotedblleft{}acchan, amma, cēṭṭan, aniyan, cēcci, aniyatti … kuṭumbaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item bare against dressed — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumba\textquotedblright{} (Kannada), \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumbaṁ\textquotedblright{} (Malayalam)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my family.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ithu ente kuṭumbamāṇŭ}.) Is \emph{kuṭumbaṁ} native Dravidian or a loan? (\textbf{A Sanskrit loan}, like \emph{iṣṭaṁ} and \emph{sukhaṁ} — and dressed in the same \textbf{‑aṁ}.) Name the six family words you already know. (\emph{Acchan, amma, cēṭṭan, aniyan, cēcci, aniyatti}.) Which of those six means \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{} as a group? (\textbf{None of them} — that's exactly the gap \emph{kuṭumbaṁ} fills.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[suhṛttŭ]{\ml{സുഹൃത്ത്} (suhṛttŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} a word built out of \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} plus \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C35-suhruthu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kuṭumbaṁ} named the group you're born into. This word names the one you choose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{സുഹൃത്ത്}} — \emph{suhṛttŭ} — \textbf{friend}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എന്റെ} \ml{സുഹൃത്താണ്}.} — \emph{ithu ente suhṛttāṇŭ.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my friend.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The everyday spoken alternative is \textbf{\ml{കൂട്ടുകാരൻ}} (\emph{kūṭṭukāran}, male) / \textbf{\ml{കൂട്ടുകാരി}} (\emph{kūṭṭukāri}, female).

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{ഹൃ}} is \textbf{\ml{ഹ}} (\emph{ha}) carrying the \textbf{\ml{ൃ}} sign — the short vocalic \emph{r} inherited straight from Sanskrit, the same vowel that opened \textbf{\ml{വൃശ്ചികം}} several chapters back. Malayalam is the only one of the four literary Dravidian scripts that still writes it as a distinct vowel sign rather than respelling it away.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സുഹൃത്ത്}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{सुहृद्}} (\emph{suhṛd}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good-heart}\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{\dv{सु}} (\emph{su}) \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{\dv{हृद्}} (\emph{hṛd}) \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} — the very root a later chapter in this same stretch meets again as \textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}}, \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} itself. Friendship, in Malayalam's borrowed word for it, is a matter of the heart before it is a matter of anything else.

Everyday speech reaches just as often for \textbf{\ml{കൂട്ടുകാരൻ}/\ml{കൂട്ടുകാരി}} — native \textbf{\ml{കൂട്ട്}} (\emph{kūṭṭŭ}, \textquotedblleft{}joining, group,\textquotedblright{} the same root as the verb \textbf{\ml{കൂടുക}}, \textquotedblleft{}to join, unite\textquotedblright{}) plus the agentive \textbf{‑\ml{കാരൻ}/‑\ml{കാരി}}. That suffix is itself borrowed, from Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{कार}} (\emph{kāra}, \textquotedblleft{}maker, doer\textquotedblright{}) fused onto a Dravidian personal ending — so even Malayalam's more casual, native-rooted word for \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{} leans on a Sanskrit-derived ending to finish the job. Selective borrowing, as \emph{santōṣaṁ} already showed back near the start of this book, does not always mean choosing one word wholesale over another; sometimes it means splicing a Dravidian root and a Sanskrit ending into a single new word.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ithu ente suhṛttāṇŭ\textquotedblright{} — this is my friend
  \item the casual alternative — \textquotedblleft{}kūṭṭukāran, kūṭṭukāri\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two pieces — \textquotedblleft{}su,\textquotedblright{} good, plus \textquotedblleft{}hṛd,\textquotedblright{} heart
  \item family and friend, one chapter — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumbaṁ … suhṛttŭ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my friend.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ithu ente suhṛttāṇŭ}.) What does \emph{suhṛttŭ} literally mean, piece by piece? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Good}\textquotedblright{} \emph{su} + \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{heart}\textquotedblright{} \emph{hṛd}.) Name the everyday spoken alternative, and what its ending is borrowed from. (\emph{Kūṭṭukāran/kūṭṭukāri} — the \textbf{‑\ml{കാരൻ}/‑\ml{കാരി}} ending is from \textbf{Sanskrit kāra}, \textquotedblleft{}maker.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
